clauses.text: Every runtime that runs the Form must produce the same results bit for bit, and the rules that make this so are checked by machine.
| `09-wellformedness.md` | the list of rules a program must pass to be accepted |
Their programs must still be accepted by the reference checker.

`rce-spec-check` (in `spec/checker/`, Rust only) reads the EBNF of section 3 from `book/03-syntax.md`, builds its LALR(1) tables and fails on any shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflict, then parses every program in `spec/examples/` and requires every program in `spec/examples/reject/` to be refused, by the LALR(1) tables, the Rust parser and the tree-sitter port alike, then runs `rce-check` over the same files (all examples together form one program and must be accepted; the 12 syntax rejects, the 48 programs in `spec/examples/ill_typed/` and the 16 in `spec/examples/inadmissible/` must be ref

On the first token of a logical line with indentation width w (number of leading spaces): if w > top, push w and emit `INDENT`; if w < top, pop while w < top and emit one `DEDENT` per pop, and w must then equal top (otherwise the text is refused: "inconsistent dedent"); if w = top, emit nothing.
The line must start with `#` in column 0 and hold, after optional spaces, `rce-version:` and a version; trailing spaces are allowed.

- **R1 dangling else.** `else` only follows a `Block` (statement `if`) or is mandatory (`if … then … else …` expression). A statement `if` ends at its `DEDENT`, so the next `else` at the same indentation belongs to it.

- **R2 `try … else` against `if … then … else`.** The branches of an `if` expression and the operands of `try` are `CatchExpr`, which cannot contain a bare `try` or `if`. `if c then try a else b` is a syntax error; write `if c then (try a else b) else d`.
- **R3 comparison chains.** `0 < a < 10` is a syntax error (non-associative). Write `a in 0..10`.
- **R4 assignment against equality.** `=` is a statement form, never an expression; `(x = 1)` is a syntax error.
- **R5 generic call against index.** `f[T](x)` parses as `index(f, T)` then a call; name resolution (4.3) turns an index of a generic function or type by type arguments into instantiation, as in Go.
- **R6 impl generics against slice types.** `impl [T] …` would be ambiguous with the slice type `[T]`, so impl parameters need `forall`: `impl forall[T: Show] Show for List[T]`.

- **R7 labels.** In argument and pattern lists `NAME ":"` is always a label. Map literals `{k: v}` are in a different bracket, so `{a: 1}` is a map whose key is the variable `a` (write `{"a": 1}` for a text key).

- **R8 variant patterns against bindings.** A `Path` pattern is a unit variant if name resolution finds a variant of that name in scope, otherwise it binds a fresh variable (Rust's rule). W-PAT-1 refuses a binding that shadows a variant name, so a misspelled variant is never silently a binding.
- **R9 send.** `<-` after an expression at statement level is a send; in prefix position it is a receive. The two never meet: `a <- <- b` is "send the value received from b to a".
2. parses the 51 programs in `examples/`, with and without their final newline; all must parse;

3. parses the 12 programs in `examples/reject/` (tab indent, chained comparison, `if` expression without `else`, `try` in a `then` branch, inconsistent dedent, `class`, assignment inside an expression, empty `kind`, state with no fields, `step` without `on`, example without `->`, unterminated string); all must be refused.
Each program is parsed three ways (the LALR(1) tables on the reference lexer's tokens, the Rust parser, and the tree-sitter port) and all three must agree.

The modules `std.text`, `std.collections` and `std.math` are built in and always resolvable (S4); a program is the set of modules given together, and `use` must name one of them or a built-in module (W-NAME-1).

**Text is byte-indexed (draft 0.5).** `s.len()` is the number of UTF-8 bytes, `s[i]` is the byte at offset i as a `u8`, and `s[a:b]` is the text between byte offsets a and b, which must both be character boundaries (otherwise `trap("not a char boundary")`).
Both operands must have the same numeric type; there is no implicit widening (use `as`).

- `step R on p if g -> e`: in context `step(R)`, the fields of R are bound as `var`, p is typed against the event sum, g : bool, and e must have the type of R's single field (only allowed when R has exactly one field;

A borrow cannot be stored in a field, a collection, a channel message, an event, a state, a closure that escapes, or be returned: with one exception: a function whose return type is a borrow (`-> &[T]`) must return a borrow derived from a parameter, and the result is tied to that parameter (R-RET).
- `chan[τ](n)` creates a channel with capacity n (a comptime or runtime usize; 0 means rendezvous) and type `chan τ`; τ must be a data type or a `chan`.
`impl Tr for T` must define every member with a signature equal to the trait's after substituting `Self := T` (W-TRAIT-1).
Coherence: at most one impl of a trait for a type in the whole program, and an impl must be in the module of the trait or of the type (orphan rule, W-TRAIT-2).
`linear struct H` declares a type whose values must be used exactly once.
It is meant for handles to outside resources (a file, a socket, a device buffer) that must be released once and only once.

`Guarded[τ, A]` is the type of a state field only (W-CAP-1); reading it gives a τ, it keeps τ's range checks (6.3), and a step that writes it (assignment, `&mut` borrow, a mutating method, or the arrow form of its only field) must match only events whose payload has a field of type `Cap[A]` (W-CAP-2).

clauses.section: 6. Dynamic semantics: the mapping into the Form
clauses.text: It also lists the exact edge behaviour of every primitive (overflow, division by zero, float rounding, text indexing), which every implementation must reproduce.
A log may also carry `outcome`, `out` and `state`; these are derived and must equal replay (T1), so they are not hashed.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N1 Numbers.** A Form number is an int (i64, or u64 per N2) or a float (finite f64). The type is part of the value and is kept across every boundary: a float with no fractional part stays a float (`10.0` is written `10.0` in canonical JSON, `10` is an int), and `-0.0` keeps its sign (N3 F6). Derivation: encoding must be injective and round-trip, `decode(encode(v)) == v`, because replay rebuilds state from D. Turning `10.0` into `10` at a boundary would decode as an int, changing the static type a later step sees and the bits of later float arithmetic, so no normalization is applied. RCE's s

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N2 Integer arithmetic** is checked: overflow of the *static type's* range is `trap("overflow: V is outside T")` with V the exact result and T the static type (`i64` for an untyped literal), never a wrap. `/` truncates toward zero (`-7 / 2 = -3`); `%` has the sign of the dividend (`-3 % 2 = -1`). Division or remainder by zero is `trap("division by zero")`. Modular and clamped arithmetic are explicit methods, never the default: `a.wrapping_add(b)`, `wrapping_sub`, `wrapping_mul` give the result modulo 2^N mapped into the static type's range, and `saturating_add`, `saturating_sub`, `saturatin

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N3 Floats.** The rules below are derived from IEEE 754-2019 and from two requirements of the Form: replay must give the same bits on every target (T1), and δ must be total (S1). `tests/float_rules.rs` checks each rule on the interpreter; the parity set carries the vectors of `examples/57_float_vectors.rce` to every CI target.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F1 Correct rounding.** f64 is IEEE binary64. `+ - * /` and `sqrt` are the standard's basic operations, correctly rounded with roundTiesToEven, the default rounding-direction attribute; so are the conversion of an integer (`as f64`) and of a decimal literal. A correctly rounded operation is a function of its operands' bits alone, so every conforming target gives the same result: this is the only property determinism needs, and no other rounding mode exists in RCE.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F2 One rounding per operator, in source order.** Float addition and multiplication are not associative and `a * b + c` with one rounding differs from two roundings (vector `MulSub`: `0.1 * 10.0 - 1.0` is `0`, fused it is `5.551115123125783e-17`). Contraction to fused multiply-add, reassociation, excess precision and every other value-changing optimization the standard allows a language to permit are therefore not valid compilations (HC-14). A fused multiply-add is itself correctly rounded, so it may exist only as an explicit named operation; RCE has none yet. Adding one needs a correctly r

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F3 Subnormals are preserved.** Gradual underflow is part of the binary64 format; flush-to-zero and denormals-are-zero modes are not IEEE operations and would make `x - y == 0` hold for `x != y`. A host never enables them (HC-13); vectors `Mul(5e-324, 3.0)` and `Mul(2.2250738585072014e-308, 0.5)` detect either mode.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F4 Non-finite results trap (from totality).** A Form value must have a reflexive equality and a total order (6.2, N5, N6) and must encode as a JSON number for hashing (N1). NaN is unequal to itself under IEEE comparison, and an infinity is not a JSON number and reintroduces NaN through `inf - inf` and `0 * inf`; the largest subset of binary64 closed under these requirements is the finite values. δ is total as a function into values and traps, so an operation whose IEEE result is not finite (the standard's overflow, divideByZero and invalid exceptions) is `trap("non-finite float")`. The alt

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F5 NaN payloads are never observable.** By F4 no NaN becomes a value, so its sign, payload and quiet bit cannot reach state, output or a hash; the standard leaves payload propagation to the implementation, which is why this matters. An implementation tests for a non-finite result before any NaN escapes, and the trap text is the same for every NaN. A fabric or target that can produce NaN (GPU, NPU, WASM SIMD) canonicalizes or traps before a value reaches state (HC-13; `wasm_float.rs` rewrites NaN to the canonical positive NaN).

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F6 Signed zero is a distinct state.** `-0.0` arises by the standard's sign rules, which are exact, so every target produces it in the same places (vector `Mul(0.0, -1.0)`). It is observable: `as f32` keeps the sign and f32 `tostr` prints `-0`, and the sign decides later results through the same exact rules. The state hash must be injective on observable state (otherwise two states a program can tell apart share a log entry), so canonical JSON keeps the sign and a state holding `-0.0` hashes differently from one holding `0.0`; this is correct, not a defect. `-0.0 == 0.0` is true (IEEE compa

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F7 Exception flags are not state.** Inexact and underflow raise nothing (F1 already fixes the result); overflow, divideByZero and invalid are the trap of F4. No program reads a flag.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F8 Exact operations.** `floor`, `ceil` and `round` are the standard's roundToIntegral operations toward negative, toward positive and ties-away (`(2.5).round()` is `3`, `(-2.5).round()` is `-3`); `abs` clears the sign. `min` and `max` follow N5. None of these rounds.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **F9 Transcendentals are excluded.** IEEE 754-2019 recommends but does not require correctly rounded `exp`, `log`, `sin`, `pow` and the like, and platform math libraries differ in the last bit. RCE has none. One may be added only with a correctly rounded implementation in the CORE-MATH or CRlibm style (correct rounding proved, or checked exhaustively for binary32), carried by every runtime rather than taken from the platform library; until then device versions are output only or verified (HC-13). Canonical float text is the shortest round-trip digits; decimal notation for 1e-5 ≤ |x| < 1e16,

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N4 Mixed arithmetic** does not exist in RCE (both operands of a binary operator have the same static type). `a as f64` converts an integer exactly when |a| ≤ 2^53 and otherwise rounds to nearest even; `x as iN` truncates toward zero and traps if the result is out of range or x is not finite.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N5 min / max** compare exactly on integers and by IEEE order on floats (total, since operands are finite); on a tie the receiver is returned.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N6 Equality** is structural value equality within one static type; `1 == 1.0` is a type error (the type is part of the value, N1). Float `==` is IEEE comparison, so `-0.0 == 0.0` although the two are distinct states (N3 F6).

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N7 Text** is a sequence of Unicode scalar values compared by code point, stored as UTF-8. From draft 0.5, `len`, indexing and slicing count UTF-8 bytes (Form `blen`, `bget`, `bslice`): `s[i]` is a `u8`, and a slice whose ends are not character boundaries is `trap("not a char boundary")`. `for c in s` and `chars()` still go by character. Case mapping (`upper`, `lower`) and class tests (`isdigit`, `isalpha`, `isupper`, `islower`) are ASCII-only; other characters are unchanged / false. `strip`, `words` and `toint` treat as whitespace exactly the 25 code points of the White_Space property of U

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N8 Indexing** The index `i` of `a[i]` and the ends of `a[i:j]` have type `usize` (W-TY-1 otherwise), so no index is negative. `a[i]` with i ≥ n is `trap("index i out of range")`. A slice end above n is `trap("slice index out of range")`, and i > j is `trap("slice bounds reversed")`; an omitted end is 0 or n. Indexing and slicing are total or trapping by one rule: an out-of-range position is never silently moved.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N9 Limits.** A list or text built by any operation is at most SIZE_LIMIT = 1,000,000 elements (`trap("size limit")`). A value written to state is at most VALUE_LIMIT = 1,048,576 bytes of canonical JSON (`trap("value limit")`, the event is refused, the value is not recorded).

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N10 Absence.** `none` and a present `()` differ, exactly as the Form's null-versus-absent rule: an option field holding none is present.

clauses.section: 6.3 Edge semantics of primitives (normative, from form/num.rs)
clauses.text: - **N11 Time** is the logical clock only: `Tick` events and `after n` in `select`. No construct reads a wall clock.
Layer 1 must be kept by every call of the cycle and shrunk by at least one; the calls it shrinks are done.
Layer 2 must be kept by every call not yet done and shrunk by at least one of them, and so on.
X` the last event is refused with X (earlier events must be applied), and for `-> e` the event list is fully applied and then
- otherwise e must be a `bool` expression over the final state, with fields in scope by name (or `R.f` when ambiguous), and must be true.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: This section is the checklist of rules a program must pass to be accepted (*well-formedness*).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-LEX-1 Not UTF-8, BOM, bare CR, or a tab character.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-LEX-2 Inconsistent dedent (2.6).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-LEX-3 A literal outside every possible type range, or an invalid `\u{}`.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-SYN-1 Not in the language of section 3.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-VER-1 A first-line `# rce-version:` declaration naming a version other than 0.5, 0.6 or 0.7 (2.7).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-NAME-1 Unresolved name, or a name resolved in the wrong namespace.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-NAME-2 Duplicate declaration in one scope; shadowing a parameter, field or module-level name inside the same item.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-MOD-1 `use` of a private item; W-MOD-2 import cycle. The reference checker reports a private name reached through `use` as W-VIS-1, which is the same rule.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-MOD-1 `use` of a private item; W-MOD-2 import cycle. The reference checker reports a private name reached through `use` as W-VIS-1, which is the same rule.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-MOD-3 An imported name that clashes with a declaration of the importing module or with a name imported from another module (imported names are not renamed).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-SAFE-1 The identifiers `unsafe`, `Rc`, `Arc`, `RefCell`, `transmute`, `static`: refused with "memory safety is by construction" (there are no escape hatches in RCE other than the `extern` boundary of 5.11).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-FFI-1 An `extern` declaration whose ABI is not `"C"`, that is comptime or generic, or whose parameter or result types break 5.11; or a foreign function's name used other than as the callee of a direct call.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-TY-1 Any typing rule of section 5 fails.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-TY-2 Nested option `τ??`; borrow of a borrow `&&τ`; `[τ]` not behind a borrow; a borrow, region type or `fn` type inside a data type.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-TY-3 Integer/float mixing without `as`; implicit narrowing.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-PAT-1 A binding pattern whose name equals a variant in scope.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-MATCH-1 A non-exhaustive `match` (5.3 [Match]); W-MATCH-2 an unreachable arm (subsumed by earlier unguarded arms).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-MATCH-1 A non-exhaustive `match` (5.3 [Match]); W-MATCH-2 an unreachable arm (subsumed by earlier unguarded arms).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-OWN-1 Use after move (O1). W-OWN-2 Violating [No-Alias-Write] or [No-Mut-Read]. W-OWN-3 Storing, returning (except R-RET) or capturing a borrow. W-REG-1 A region-typed value escaping its `with arena` block.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-SPAWN-1 Spawning with a borrow or region-typed argument.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-STATE-1 A `state` with no fields; W-STATE-2 a field initializer that is not a comptime constant; W-STATE-3 a field type that is not an owned data type.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-STATE-1 A `state` with no fields; W-STATE-2 a field initializer that is not a comptime constant; W-STATE-3 a field type that is not an owned data type.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-STATE-1 A `state` with no fields; W-STATE-2 a field initializer that is not a comptime constant; W-STATE-3 a field type that is not an owned data type.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-STEP-1 A `step` naming an undeclared region or matching an undeclared event. W-STEP-2 **Totality**: an event that no step and no actor handler can ever match. W-STEP-3 The arrow form on a region with more than one field. W-STEP-4 Within one region, two unguarded steps whose patterns overlap (the second is unreachable).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-EFF-1 `emit`, `spawn`, channel operations or `select` in a pure `fn`; reading another region's fields in a step; calling a foreign function anywhere but `fn main` or a task function.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-REC-1 A cycle in the call graph, including through trait methods after monomorphization, other than a cycle of plain functions (one function calling itself included) whose calls are done by layered summed measures, or each of whose cycles of calls passes through a function declared with `bound` (6.7); `par` or `for … par` in a function of a cycle with a bounded function; `bound` on an iterator, a foreign function or a trait signature.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-CT-1 Comptime code that calls a non-comptime-safe function or traps or exceeds fuel.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-INT-1 An `example` or `check` that does not hold.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-SIMD-1 A lane-wise operator on arrays of different lengths, of an unfixed length, or with non-numeric lanes (5.1).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-LIN-1 A linear value not consumed exactly once on every path, copied, moved inside a loop, or placed in a collection, field, payload, channel or iterator (5.12).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-DEV-1 A growable value (`List`, `Map`, `Set`, `text`, slice, channel, iterator) bound in a device region, or `emit`, `spawn`, send, `select`, `yield` or a foreign call inside one (5.13).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-ITER-1 An iterator function that is not pure or has an arrow body; `yield` outside an iterator function; an `iter τ` value used other than as a `for` operand or `.collect()` receiver (5.14).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-REF-1 A refined type (5.1) that is generic, refines a type other than an integer type, `text` or a collection, or whose predicate is outside the decidable fragment (a term other than `self`, `self.len()` or an integer literal, an operator other than a comparison, `and`, `or`, `not`, or a call other than a text character class).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-LOOP-1 A `LOOP_LIMIT` declaration that is not `const LOOP_LIMIT: u64 = n` with a positive literal n (6.7).

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-TRAIT-1 An impl not matching its trait; W-TRAIT-2 incoherent or orphan impls; W-TRAIT-3 a type used with `==`, `!=`, an ordering operator or a generic bound without implementing the trait it needs.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-TRAIT-1 An impl not matching its trait; W-TRAIT-2 incoherent or orphan impls; W-TRAIT-3 a type used with `==`, `!=`, an ordering operator or a generic bound without implementing the trait it needs.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-TRAIT-1 An impl not matching its trait; W-TRAIT-2 incoherent or orphan impls; W-TRAIT-3 a type used with `==`, `!=`, an ordering operator or a generic bound without implementing the trait it needs.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-CTX-1 Context text made other than by `C.lit` of a string literal or `C.encode`; joined with another context or plain text; carried by an event payload; an unknown context.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-SEC-1 An operator or method on a secret other than `==`/`!=`; a secret in an emitted value, a channel, an error payload or a foreign call.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-CAP-1 A capability outside an event payload field or a parameter; `Guarded` outside a state field; an authority that is not a declared struct.

clauses.section: 7. Well-formedness: what is refused at entry
clauses.text: - W-CAP-2 A step that writes a `Guarded[τ, A]` field on an event without a `Cap[A]` field. (W-NAME-2 refuses a declaration named after a 5.16 type or context.)

| T1 | proved for expressions, δ, and the 6.8 tick semantics (tasks, channels, select, actors): one tick from a configuration has exactly one result | `step_det`, `exec_unique`, `tstep_det`, `run_det`, `tick_det` |

| T2 | proved, including the explicit bound: a statement reaches its `exec` result in at most B(s) steps (B from loop bounds and expression sizes), a region in at most BR, δ in at most |s|·BR(P). The Lean expression core has no user function calls. Structural recursion (0.4) is proved separately on a model with total leaf and combine bodies: fuel equal to the value's size always suffices, the result equals the function's denotation, extra fuel changes nothing, and the number of calls equals the size. Mutual recursion (6.7) is proved on a model of a family of functions whose calls lower a measu
| T3 | proved | `fold_law`, `log_is_events`, `replay` |

| T4 | proved for expressions, statements, δ and ticks (some task moves, or every task is done or blocked: the run ends or is `Deadlock`) | `progress`, `stmt_progress`, `delta_bound`, `run_progress`, `progress` (Conc) |

The rule that decides what needs a new version: a module's meaning (its outputs, states and outcomes, including where a budget traps) must be determined by its declared version, so a change that gives a valid program of an existing version a different meaning that the old text defined is a new version; a change that makes the implementations meet text that already defined the meaning, or that only touches artifacts outside a program's meaning, is an erratum and applies to every version.

This appendix states what a host must do to run an RCE program.

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-1 One admitter per term.** At any log height a program instance has exactly one admitter, the holder of the current term (E.2b). Every input reaches δ only after the admitter appended it to D, in D's order. The admitter is a role, not a machine: when it fails, another host takes the role for a higher term and continues the same D (E.2b). A host without replication holds term 0 for its lifetime, which is the single admitter of earlier versions.

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-2 Only the admitter reads clocks.** Wall time and monotonic time enter only as events (`Tick(n)`, and `host.WallTime` when an adapter supplies it). Time inside the language is logical (6.3 N11, C.11.12).

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-3 Typed output requests.** Each effect requested by λ (a write, a send, a draw, a foreign call) has exactly one result event: delivered, failed, timed out or unreachable. A race inside the adapter (for example a file checked and then opened) is resolved by the adapter; the program sees one atomic outcome.

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-4 Foreign code.** Foreign code runs only through 5.11, with its arguments copied or borrowed for the call only, under fuel, and its result or trap logged as `Foreign(f, arguments, result)`. An isolated component boundary (a WebAssembly component per call) is the recommended adapter; it does not change the rule.

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-5 Capabilities.** Authority comes only from capabilities minted by logged events (5.16 `Cap[A]` in a version 0.8 module). The host holds no ambient authority on the program's behalf. This is the sandbox, and its contract is independent of any OS: the checker admits only programs whose effects go through granted capabilities, and the deterministic host refuses any effect without one, before any OS layer is involved. The same contract then has enforcement targets underneath the host, entered at start as strictly as the target allows: WASM (the module imports only the granted host function

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-6 Tick scheduler.** Concurrency runs under the tick semantics of 6.8. The host runs `fn main` (tasks, actors, supervisors; C.5, C.13) with its scheduler as a live task whose every transition is an entry of D. `host.MainStart` {links, max_ticks, seed} starts the task; `host.MainInput` {a, b, partition, tick} logs an input to it (a link change), and `host.MainInput` {event, tick} feeds it a program event (canonical event JSON): at that tick the scheduler logs `Input(..)` and delivers the event to every live actor whose type has an `on` handler for it, in actor-id order, or logs `Unhandled

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-7 Numerics and limits.** The host reproduces 6.3 bit for bit and enforces fuel, SIZE_LIMIT and VALUE_LIMIT (6.7, N9) as the reference does, on every run.

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-7a Fuel per input.** A host is event driven, so fuel is charged per admitted input: each input (one application of δ, including constructing its event) starts with the full fuel of 6.7, and no budget is shared across inputs. Every input has its own bound and a session never starves however long it runs. The reference trace (`rce trace`), the host and replay all reset fuel per input, so a refusal for fuel is a function of that input and the state before it, and D is the same on each.

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-8 Replay.** A host offers a replay mode that reads D, disconnects every adapter and re-derives every state hash. Replay reads no clock, file, network, device or environment (T37).

clauses.section: E.2 Admission, time and authority (HC-1 to HC-9)
clauses.text: - **HC-9 Priority admission.** Interrupt sources carry a priority in 0..255 (T25, C.11.12). Inputs admitted together are ordered by priority, highest first. Inputs with a source and sequence number are ordered by the window key of HC-15. Inputs given together without source identity (`admit_simultaneous`) are ordered by priority, then by the bytes of their canonical event JSON, so the order is a function of the set of inputs and not of the order the caller passed them in. Either way the order chosen is D's order. A real-time bound holds only on a kernel with a priority scheduler; a general-pur
The order of D must not depend on when inputs arrive.

- **HC-15 Windows.** Every input carries its source id (text), a per-source sequence number (1, 2, ... with no reuse) and the logical tick its source stamped on it. When the module declares `event Tick(n: u64)`, a window closes when a `Tick(n)` input not yet in D is offered: window k gets `upto = n`, holds every offered input with tick at most `upto` that is not already in D, and the `Tick(n)` is its last input. The boundary is therefore a logged fact, never a wall clock and never a choice of the caller. An input whose tick is at or below the `upto` of the last window in D is late: it is admit

- **HC-16 Exactly once.** The dedupe key is (source, seq). A (source, seq) already in D, or offered twice, is a duplicate and is not appended again. Two copies of one (source, seq) with different payloads are ordered by their event bytes, and the lower one is admitted, so the choice does not depend on arrival. An input after a gap in its source's sequence is held for a later window, so each source is admitted in its own order and nothing is skipped. - **HC-17 Window entries.** Closing a window appends `host.Window` {count, id, term, upto}, then, before each admitted input, `host.Input` {late (only when true), seq, source, window}. The dedupe state is the fold of these entries: on open and on replay the admitter rebuilds, per source, the highest seq in D. A `host.Input` counts only when the program entry it announces follows it, so a cut between the two (HS-4) admits nothing. These are host entries: δ never reads them and they leave the state hash unchanged.

clauses.section: E.2b Replicated D and admitter failover (HC-18 to HC-20)
clauses.text: - **HC-18 Interface.** A replicated log offers the host the Store of E.3 with two additions: `elect(term)`, which succeeds only with grants from a quorum of replicas, each of which then promises not to accept an append from a lower term, and returns the most up-to-date log among the granting quorum, ordered by (term of the last write, length); and an append at a term that a replica accepts only while it has promised no higher term. The barrier succeeds only when a quorum accepted every entry up to it, so a durable entry (HS-2) is a committed entry.

clauses.section: E.2b Replicated D and admitter failover (HC-18 to HC-20)
clauses.text: - **HC-19 Term fence in D.** A host that won `elect(t)` folds the log it received (HS-4 verification of the whole chain, then HC-8), then appends `host.Term` {leader, term} and makes it durable before admitting any input. `t` must exceed every term already in D. Every `host.Window` carries the term. A request emitted under an older term with no result in D gets one result, `failed` with `interrupted` (HC-3). The term in D is the fence token: an entry of D was appended by the holder of the most recent `host.Term` before it.

clauses.section: E.2b Replicated D and admitter failover (HC-18 to HC-20)
clauses.text: - **HC-18a Transport.** Replication follows Raft's AppendEntries and RequestVote: an append carries (prev_idx, prev_term) and a follower refuses it unless its log has an entry at prev_idx with that term (log matching), deletes a conflicting suffix and appends what is missing. The current term and the vote are written to stable storage before a candidate asks for votes, before a vote is granted, and before an append is acknowledged. A vote goes only to a candidate whose log is at least as up-to-date by (last term, last index). The leader advances the commit index only over entries of its own te

clauses.section: E.2b Replicated D and admitter failover (HC-18 to HC-20)
clauses.text: - **HC-20 Deposed admitter.** An admitter whose barrier is refused because a higher term was granted has had its role taken. By HS-3 it appends nothing further and acks nothing, so its unacked inputs are retransmitted to the new admitter and HC-16 removes those that did commit. Committed entries are never removed: the new admitter's log contains every entry a quorum had accepted, so D after a failover extends D before it.

**HC-10.** Every value that enters a run is an event or a logged answer in D. This includes key, pointer, resize and focus input; `Tick` and `host.WallTime`; every file, network, PTY, audio and GPU readback result; foreign results and traps; `select nondet` choices; Delivered, TimedOut and Unreachable; capability minting; lifecycle (suspend, resume, process kill); random bytes; and the host entries of E.5. An input that is not in D does not exist for the program.

clauses.section: E.6 Fabrics and placement (HC-11 to HC-14)
clauses.text: - **HC-11 Fabric discovery as events.** At start and on hot-plug the host appends `host.FabricCaps`: ISA flags, each GPU adapter's features and float controls (rounding mode, denormal preservation, signed zero, inf and NaN preservation per width), NPU receipts, memory topology and which counters can be read. Replay reads the same record, so every decision taken from it is a function of D.

clauses.section: E.6 Fabrics and placement (HC-11 to HC-14)
clauses.text: - **HC-12 Automatic placement.** The engine places each lane-wise array operation, `for … par` body and reduction itself, from the cost table of C.6.4 extended with per-fabric overhead and throughput (time = overhead + work / throughput), whose calibration results are `host.Calibrated` entries. A program needs no annotation. `with device` (5.13) and device kernels stay hints that never change meaning. Placement is a function of the host entries of D, so it is the same on replay (T37): the host logs each decision as `host.Placed` and replay re-derives it and refuses D when it differs. A fabric

clauses.section: E.6 Fabrics and placement (HC-11 to HC-14)
clauses.text: - **HC-13 Bit-exactness gate.** A fabric computes a value that reaches state only for an operation on its logged exact list: integer operations; IEEE add, sub, mul, div and sqrt with round-to-nearest-even, no contraction and no flush to zero; and reductions in the fixed tree of T18. An operation enters the list by a probe whose digest equals the CPU reference digest, logged as `host.Exact`. Everything else (transcendentals, vendor BLAS, f16, NPU, any WGSL float operation, whose rounding WGSL does not specify) is either output only (λ sinks) or verified: recomputed on the reference, or checked

clauses.section: E.6 Fabrics and placement (HC-11 to HC-14)
clauses.text: - **HC-14 No performance flags.** No user-visible setting chooses performance. The engine derives the build profile (optimization, link time optimization, codegen units, target ISA from `host.FabricCaps`), the allocator and collection policy and the I/O backend. A knob is admissible only when it cannot change meaning (decision 38; 10.1). Fast math, floating contraction, excess precision and hash-seed randomization do not exist under the contract. - **TU-1 (proposed).** Every primitive value is an n-dimensional tensor `Tensor[elem, shape]`, where `elem` is one of the primitive element types of 5.1 and `shape` is a list of non-negative dimensions. A scalar is the rank 0 tensor `Tensor[elem, []]`. Relation: generalizes the primitive types of 5.1; a version 0.5 to 0.8 program keeps its meaning because each of its scalars is read as rank 0.

- **TU-2 (proposed).** The shape is part of the type and is checked statically. An operation whose operand shapes do not agree (for example a matrix product of `[m, k]` and `[j, n]` with k not equal to j) is a checker error, never a run-time trap. Dimensions are literals or names bound in the signature; a shape that cannot be determined statically is refused. Relation: a new W-rule in 9 when adopted.

- **TU-3 (proposed).** A record whose fields all have one element type and one shape may be read as a tensor over a named axis (`{x: f64, y: f64}` as `Tensor[f64, [axis: {x, y}]]`). Field names index that axis. A record with mixed field types stays a record.

- **TU-4 (proposed).** Every reduction over an axis follows N-9: a left fold over the axis in index order unless the program names a different fixed tree. The shape and the named tree, never the thread count or fabric, determine the bits.
- **TU-5 (proposed).** Text, maps, graphs and sum types remain separate canonical values. They are ragged and are never padded or densified into tensors; a tensor element is never one of them.
- **TU-6 (proposed).** Placement (HC-12) keys the fabric cost table by (pure operation, element type, shape). Choosing a fabric changes cost only; HC-7 and N-9 fix the result bits.
